# Q.1
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lessR)
library(readxl)
library(BSDA)
b_p <- read_xlsx("butterflies_pesticides.xlsx")
groups  <- b_p[[1]]
wing_length <- b_p[[2]]
cntrl_length <- wing_length[groups == "group1"]
exp_length <- wing_length[groups == "group2"]
shapiro.test(cntrl_length)
shapiro.test(exp_length)
```
# Q.2
```{r}
cntrl_group <- b_p$`Wing Length`[b_p$Group =="group1"]
exp_group <- b_p$`Wing Length`[b_p$Group =="group2"]
var.test(cntrl_group, exp_group)
```
# Q.3
```{r}
t.test(cntrl_group, exp_group, var.equal = FALSE)
```
# Q.4
```{r}
boxplot(cntrl_group, exp_group, 
        main = "Wing length in butterflies exposed to pestices",
        xlab = "Control group                                 Pesticide group",
        ylab = "Wing length",
        col = "lightblue",
        border = "darkblue"
)
```
# Q.5
```{r}
# I analyzed if there was a difference in wing length between butterflies exposed or not to pesticides. I started by doing a Shapiro test for normality for both the experimental and control group, the results showed that both are distributed normally ( control group p-value = 0.146; experimental group p-value = 0.6247). An equal variance test was done between the groups and results showed that there were significant differences in their variance (p-value = 0.005512). To see if there are significant differences between the groups a Welch two sample t-test was done; results suggest that there is difference within the groups (p-value = 0.000172). Visualizing the data with a box plot it is clear that the the experimental groups shows a typically shorter wing length. All these results suggest that exposure to pesticides prevents butterflies from growing their wings to the same length controls can.
```
